chunks.content: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY Well-characterised sarcoidosis cases with focus on pulmonary involvement and longitudinal follow-up to assess progression. Use of an ex vivo sarcoidosis granuloma model with advanced omics techniques to identify the biomarkers and mechanisms of early granuloma formation that may provide keys to progressive disease. Robust study design to develop a classification model along with validation in an independent cohort of sarcoidosis cases. Limitations include the focus on a rare disease, sarcoidosis, with inherent heterogeneity of clinical presentation and potential for occult systemic disease, which may require a larger study population to achieve adequate power to detect signals of pulmonary disease progression. Introduction Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease of unknown cause, with variable and unpredictable severity and outcomes. It affects an estimated 45–300 per 100 000 individuals in the USA and occurs across all ages, population groups and sexes. Annual mortality is estimated to be at least 2.8/million people and highest among African American women at 18.7/million and overall sarcoidosis-associated mortality is rising. Respiratory failure remains the leading cause of sarcoidosis-related mortality. Lung involvement occurs in more than 90% of patients, yet disease trajectories differ substantially: some individuals experience chronic inflammation with progressive pulmonary fibrosis culminating in respiratory failure, whereas others undergo spontaneous resolution. Despite incremental advances that distinguish sarcoidosis from healthy controls, the biological factors driving these divergent phenotypes remain poorly understood, and no validated biomarkers exist to identify individuals at risk of progressive disease. Genetic and environmental factors contribute to heterogeneity in sarcoidosis outcomes. For example, Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-DRB10301 strongly predicts a benign, self-limited phenotype (non-progressive sarcoidosis, NP-sarcoidosis) among Swedish patients with Löfgren syndrome, who typically do not require treatment. In contrast, Swedish Löfgren patients carrying other HLA genotypes—including DRB10101, *0401, *1301, and *1501—are more likely to develop progressive disease (progressive sarcoidosis (P-sarcoidosis)) and require therapy. These genotype–phenotype associations, however, do not generalise to diverse, admixed populations such as those in the USA, where polygenic architecture and racial variation complicate prediction of clinical course. Blood-based gene expression signatures involving T-cell receptor signalling and CXCL9 have been proposed to differentiate progressive from non-progressive phenotypes, but remain of limited clinical utility and lack validation in independent cohorts. The lack of reliable, tractable biomarkers continues to impede both clinical decision-making and research progress in sarcoidosis. For example, sarcoidosis clinical trials have found limited differences in treated and placebo groups, with concerns raised that individuals enrolled are remitting or stable and not always progressing. Existing studies have primarily compared sarcoidosis cases to healthy controls, a strategy that obscures the substantial clinical heterogeneity that defines this disease and defines differences that may not have clinical impact to flag those with more severe disease. P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis represent clinically divergent phenotypes with markedly different prognoses and treatment needs, yet no validated biomarkers exist to distinguish them. Preliminary data from our group indicate that P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis may be differentiated by blood-derived and peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC)-derived molecular signatures—especially proteins linked to granuloma biogenesis—suggesting the presence of biologically meaningful, clinically useful subtype-specific signals. To address this critical gap, the present study employs a fundamentally different approach that focuses directly on P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis, rather than case–control contrasts. We use an integrative, data-driven strategy combining proteomic and transcriptomic analyses across multiple biological compartments—including an ex vivo granuloma model, PBMCs and plasma—to comprehensively characterise pathways driving granuloma formation and disease persistence. We hypothesised that a molecular systems biology approach will provide novel insights into the P-sarcoidosis phenotype, identifying robust molecular signatures linked to granuloma formation and pragmatic features predictive of disease progression. No prior study outside our preliminary work has evaluated the proteomic landscape of progressive sarcoidosis at this depth. By integrating multi-omic data, we aim to uncover biological mechanisms that cannot be identified by single-platform analyses and to identify blood-based molecular markers readily translatable to clinical practice. Methods and analysis Objectives The goal of this project is to leverage broad gene expression and protein-level data to identify mechanisms of pulmonary sarcoidosis progression and to build a classification model for progressive pulmonary sarcoidosis in plasma. Primary goal: To develop and validate a multimodal classification model that will predict pulmonary sarcoidosis progression. Secondary goal: Integrate gene expression and proteomic changes in circulating PBMCs as well as a well-established ex vivo granuloma model using circulating PBMCs to identify novel mechanisms linked to pulmonary sarcoidosis progression. To address these goals, we proposed the following study aims ( ): Aim 1: Characterise protein and gene expression profiles in the established ex vivo granuloma model to identify signatures of granuloma formation in progressive pulmonary sarcoidosis. Aim 2: Integrate PBMC proteomics with RNA sequencing to discover pathways and signatures of progressive sarcoidosis. Aim 3: Develop and validate a comprehensive model to predict progressive disease based on plasma proteins, clinical variables and patient reported outcomes (PROs). Eligibility criteria

Eligibility criteria We will recruit sarcoidosis cases who meet rigorous eligibility criteria ( ), aligning with the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society criteria for a diagnosis of sarcoidosis Statement or have highly probable clinical diagnosis criteria. Participants will have been diagnosed within 4.5 years of enrolment. Participants with fibrotic (chest X-ray (CXR) stage IV) lung disease will be excluded if there are no findings to suggest an inflammatory component to their pulmonary disease. The sarcoidosis cases will be included if they are not on systemic anti-inflammatory therapy, except hydroxychloroquine or prednisone ≤10 mg/day or equivalent doses of steroids. Box 1 Study eligibility criteria Inclusion Biopsy proven granulomatous lung disease, with exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation (such as CBD, common variable immunodeficiency, mycobacterial and/or fungal infection or suspected hypersensitivity pneumonitis, etc) as per the ATS criteria. In case of extra-pulmonary biopsy, providing evidence of granulomatous inflammation, abnormal chest imaging (either CXR or CT) is needed for evidence of pulmonary involvement. For the Discovery Cohort, we will enrol subjects within 4 years of diagnosis, with pulmonary involvement including those with radiographic Scadding Stage 0 (no pulmonary disease on CXR, but with biopsy and/or CT confirmation of lung involvement), I (lymphadenopathy on CXR but no parenchymal disease), II (lymphadenopathy and parenchymal disease on CXR) or III (no lymphadenopathy but parenchymal disease on CXR) disease, and those with Stage IV disease if they have evidence of nodules, ground glass or other findings to suggest an inflammatory component to their disease either on lung CT, CXR or PET scan. People who formerly smoked (quit >6 months ago) or people who have never smoked, including marijuana smoking and e-cigarettes/vaping. Prednisone or other corticosteroids equivalent to ≤10 mg/day or hydroxychloroquine for sarcoidosis is allowed. Other severe extra-pulmonary organ involvement that will be the sole driver of treatment without significant pulmonary disease or need for pulmonary therapy that will preclude assessment of pulmonary phenotypes. This could include severe cardiac, neurologic or other organ involvement that will require treatment in the absence of treatment indication for pulmonary disease. Study design and participants This multicentre, observational case-comparison study will enrol participants at three sites: National Jewish Health, Denver, Colorado, USA; The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio, USA; and the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA ( ). We will prospectively enrol sarcoidosis cases in a diverse discovery cohort. Participants with pulmonary sarcoidosis will be followed for two years and grouped as non-progressive (NP) or progressive (P) sarcoidosis based on changes in pulmonary function tests (PFTs), CXR or need for treatment ( ). The study will enrol 220 sarcoidosis cases for use across the study in the discovery cohort as follows: (a) n=40 subjects for the granuloma model, (b) an additional 40 or n=80 (40 P/40 NP) for PBMCs for integrated proteomics and transcriptomics profiling and (c) another 140 cases for a total of 220 to define a classifier. We will overenrol to account for potential dropouts and a small percentage of subjects who may not be classifiable as P-sarcoidosis or NP-sarcoidosis, with an expected distribution of 100 each for P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis for classifier development. The first participant was enrolled in September 2023 and we anticipate the last study participant to be enrolled in August 2026 and the two-year follow-up for phenotyping in P-sarcoidosis versus NP-sarcoidosis to be completed in August 2028. The validation cohort will be derived from prior National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute (NHLBI) studies, including subjects enrolled before treatment in a nicotine treatment trial (n=100), and participants enrolled at National Jewish Health (NJH) in sarcoidosis R01 studies (n>100), NJH sarcoidosis biobank and the University of Minnesota Sarcoidosis Registry. Box 2 Pulmonary+sarcoidosis phenotypes Progressive pulmonary disease A ≥10% decline in FVC and/or FEV1 or a ≥15% decline in DLCO. Worsening chest radiography as determined by the interpreting radiologist/investigator. Need for immunosuppressive therapy for treatment of pulmonary sarcoidosis, including corticosteroids (eg, prednisone, prednisolone, dexamethasone, etc), steroid sparing agents (eg, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, leflunomide, azathioprine, etc), biologics including anti-TNF (eg, infliximab, adalimumab, etc) and anti-B cell therapy (rituximab) and others used for sarcoidosis. No resolution of disease. Non-progressive pulmonary disease A ≤10% decline in FVC or FEV1 and a ≤15% decline in DLCO (stable) and/or ≥10% improvement in FVC or a ≥15% improvement in DLCO (improved). A stable or improved chest radiograph as determined by the interpreting radiologist/investigator. No indication for immunosuppressive therapy as outlined above. DLCO, diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide; FEV1: forced expiratory volume in the first second; FVC, forced vital capacity; TNF, tumour necrosis factor; UIP, usual interstitial pneumonitis. Study procedures and timeline Study participants will undergo procedures outlined in and . CXR and PFTs will be obtained at 12 and 24 months of follow-up for research purposes if they have not already been performed for clinical indications. Biospecimen collection: A one-time blood draw will be performed at the enrolment visit (V1) to isolate plasma and PBMCs, following standardised operating procedures across all three enrolment sites to reduce variability. At the Ohio State University (OSU), a subset of participants will undergo a large-volume blood collection to support an ex vivo granuloma model that requires freshly isolated PBMCs processed on the day of acquisition. Plasma will be processed into small-volume aliquots and stored without freeze–thaw cycles for downstream analyses, while PBMCs will be isolated and preserved either as dry pellets for proteomic studies or in RNAlater for RNA-sequencing. Although samples have been previously banked, existing cohorts do not contain PBMCs suitable for Aims 1 and 2, which necessitate fresh cells; therefore, these banked samples will be used solely as a validation cohort, for which plasma and clinical data are sufficient. Patient-reported outcome measures and questionnaires: Participants will complete three validated patient-reported outcome instruments at enrolment and every six months thereafter. Patient-reported outcome measures and questionnaires: Participants will complete three validated patient-reported outcome instruments at enrolment and every six months thereafter. These include the Medical Outcomes Study Short Form-12 to evaluate health-related quality of life, the University of California San Diego Shortness of Breath Questionnaire to assess dyspnoea and the Fatigue Assessment Scale to quantify fatigue. All measures have been previously validated in populations with sarcoidosis. In addition, occupational and environmental exposure history will be documented at baseline, including smoking status, using the GRADS (Genomic Research in Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency and Sarcoidosis) questionnaire. Physiological assessment: Pulmonary function testing—including measurements of forced vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in one second and single-breath diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide—will be performed at baseline (V1) and subsequently at 12 month follow-up visits (V3 and V5). When these assessments are not completed as part of routine clinical care, they will be obtained for study purposes. PFTs at the 6-month (V2) and 18-month (V4) visits will be optional. All testing procedures will follow established American Thoracic Society standards. Radiology : Anterior–posterior chest radiographs will be obtained at the baseline visit (V1) and again at 12 months (V3) and 24 months (V5), unless a clinically indicated film has already been performed at those time points. All images will be interpreted by a radiologist affiliated with the study site. When a chest CT scan is acquired for clinical care, a research-specific chest X-ray will not be collected. The interpretation of the radiologist will be used to determine if there is worsening, improvement or stability. Clinical phenotyping and data collection from medical records : Relevant study information will be collected from each participant’s medical record, including disease duration, pulmonary function test results, chest X-ray Scadding stage, CT imaging reports, biopsy findings and details regarding current and prior medications. As part of the IRB-approved consent procedure, participants will complete a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) authorisation form permitting the research team to access and extract the necessary clinical data. All information obtained by the investigators will be de-identified and assigned a unique study identifier. These records if in paper version, along with signed consent forms, will be securely stored in a locked filing cabinet within the investigator’s office at each study location. Data management and repository : Clinical and questionnaire data will be entered by study personnel at each clinical site into a secure Research Electronic Data Capture database (REDCap), with participants also able to complete patient-reported outcomes through linked electronic surveys. The system, hosted at NJH, is an encrypted, password-protected, web-based platform. Built-in screening tools include automated eligibility checks, and the database captures demographic information, clinical characteristics, medication and medical history, lung function results, radiologic findings and other study-specific assessments. Participants receive authenticated survey links directly for questionnaire completion, with a paper option available for those who prefer to complete forms by hand. Data quality oversight includes routine monitoring to ensure accuracy, completeness and consistency of REDCap-entered information. Automated validation rules—such as predefined ranges and missing-data flags—are applied to identify potential errors or outliers. Regular data queries will be issued to sites to resolve discrepancies, and periodic audits will be conducted to verify data accuracy and completeness across all participating centres. Molecular characterisation of the granuloma model: PBMCs will be examined ex vivo after incubation with clinical-grade Mycobacterium tuberculosis -derived immunogenic antigens, that is, purified protein derivative (PPD)-coated beads or albumin-coated bead controls, thereby mimicking key aspects of early granuloma formation. In this model, at day 7 of incubation, PBMCs from sarcoidosis patients form structured granuloma-like aggregates that reproduce the canonical Th1-skewed cytokine milieu and transcriptional programmes regulating granuloma formation, similar to those in the diseased lung. Using this approach, we will compare transcriptional programmes and protein interaction networks between sarcoidosis and NP sarcoidosis at day 7 of incubation with PPD-simulation or under control conditions of incubation with albumin-coated beads. Molecular characterisation of PBMCs and plasma: We will perform a comprehensive characterisation of circulating PBMCs and plasma to identify molecular pathways that distinguish progressive from non-progressive sarcoidosis. Parallel analyses will be performed on circulating PBMCs to identify systemic molecular signatures linked to disease progression. To develop a predictive model of progressive pulmonary disease, we will also perform comprehensive discovery-based plasma proteomic profiling within the discovery cohort and integrate protein data with clinical variables. The resulting model will then be validated in an independent validation cohort using a targeted mass spectrometry platform. plasma: We will perform a comprehensive characterisation of circulating PBMCs and plasma to identify molecular pathways that distinguish progressive from non-progressive sarcoidosis. Parallel analyses will be performed on circulating PBMCs to identify systemic molecular signatures linked to disease progression. To develop a predictive model of progressive pulmonary disease, we will also perform comprehensive discovery-based plasma proteomic profiling within the discovery cohort and integrate protein data with clinical variables. The resulting model will then be validated in an independent validation cohort using a targeted mass spectrometry platform. Analysis plan To define molecular pathways underlying progressive versus non-progressive sarcoidosis, we will compare protein abundance and gene-expression profiles from PBMCs stimulated in the ex vivo granuloma model. Differential analyses by limma and DESeq with appropriate statistical thresholds will identify proteins and transcripts that distinguish the two groups, followed by pathway-enrichment and multi-omic network-integration approaches such as ActivePathway and MARINa to reveal biologically relevant processes and upstream regulatory factors. Single-cell RNA-sequencing from a subset of samples will refine implicated immune cell populations and inform interpretation of bulk transcriptional data. Together, these analyses will establish the key pathways and regulatory programmes associated with granulomatous responses, and selected features will be carried forward to improve downstream plasma-based classifiers. With 20 progressive and 20 non-progressive cases, we have 80% power to detect meaningful differences in protein abundance (Cohen’s d ≈ 1.4; ~1.3 fold change) and gene expression (~2 fold change) at α=0.001, consistent with effect sizes observed in our prior sarcoidosis studies. Network-level approaches further enhance power by aggregating coordinated molecular signals, making it highly unlikely that multiple differentially regulated genes or proteins would cluster within a pathway by chance. We will conduct parallel analyses in circulating PBMCs using bulk RNA-sequencing together with comprehensive assessments of protein abundance to identify molecular programmes that differ between P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis. Subsequent pathway-enrichment and network-level analyses will define differentially regulated biological pathways and protein-interaction networks associated with disease progression. To build and validate a plasma classifier, we will compare plasma protein profiles between P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis and develop a classifier that reliably distinguishes the two groups. We will evaluate both individual differentially abundant proteins and the combined discriminatory power of multi-protein panels. Classifier development will proceed by first screening candidate clinical variables, patient-reported outcomes, and protein markers using univariate logistic regression, followed by multivariable elastic net modelling to identify a stable and parsimonious predictor set while controlling for overfitting. Three models—clinical features alone, protein features alone and a combined model—will be generated and compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC)-based performance metrics, including the area under the curve, to determine the most accurate approach for distinguishing P-sarcoidosis from NP-sarcoidosis. Study timeline : Recruitment began in November 2023, with a projected completion of study visits by February 2028. Patient and public involvement: While it was not possible to involve patients or the public in the design, conduct, reporting, or dissemination plans of our research, we reviewed research and white papers that indicated patient preferences to help ensure patient needs were considered. We are including patient-reported outcomes as these are relevant to patient outcomes. Discussion This study is designed to address a critical unmet need in sarcoidosis: the lack of reliable biomarkers to distinguish P-sarcoidosis from NP-sarcoidosis. By focusing directly on P-sarcoidosis and NP-sarcoidosis and applying a multi-omic strategy across PBMCs, plasma and an ex vivo granuloma model, this protocol takes a fundamentally different approach to identifying clinically meaningful disease signatures. Integrating proteomic and transcriptomic analyses enables comprehensive characterisation of pathways associated with granuloma biogenesis and disease persistence and provides an opportunity to uncover biological mechanisms that may not be detectable using single-platform analyses. A major strength of this study is its emphasis on clinically relevant phenotypes with clear implications for prognosis and treatment decision-making. The multi-compartment design—spanning cellular, secreted and modelled granulomatous environments—strengthens biological inference and enhances the likelihood of identifying reproducible markers of progression. Our focus on proteomics is particularly significant, given that protein-level dysregulation more directly reflects immune effector function and represents a set of targets with translational and therapeutic potential. Moreover, the study’s data-driven analytic framework increases the likelihood of identifying novel disease pathways and developing a classifier with direct applicability to clinical practice. This study also has anticipated limitations. Molecular signatures identified in PBMCs, plasma or ex vivo granuloma models may not fully capture the complexity of granulomatous inflammation in tissue compartments such as lung or lymph nodes. Although our multi-compartment approach mitigates this limitation, validation in independent cohorts and across diverse populations will be required for broad generalisability. Additionally, as proteomic and transcriptomic datasets are high-dimensional, classifier development may be influenced by sample size constraints, rigorous statistical controls and external validation. Finally, the results of this study will require prospective assessment in a larger cohort to evaluate changes over time. Ethics and dissemination This multicentre study is

Ethics and dissemination This multicentre study is conducted in accordance with globally accepted standards of good practice and the Declaration of Helsinki, as well as local institutional regulations. The study protocol has been approved by the Biomedical Research Alliance of New York, serving as a single IRB for the project (IRB # 23–02-503), as well as at National Jewish Health (IRB# HS-4091), University of Minnesota (STUDY00020121/SITE00002051) and The Ohio State University (IRB# 2023X0140). All participants are required to provide written informed consent. All manuscripts resulting from the study will be submitted to peer-reviewed journals. Findings will be disseminated via journal publications, scientific conferences, patient advocacy group online content, and social media platforms as permitted by the funder and the institutions where the work will be performed.
